whyNext: Builds on exact binary search from Binary Search (Seq 51) by implementing upper-bound binary search with modular wrap-around to find the smallest character strictly greater than target.
hints: Use binary search over the sorted characters to find the first character strictly greater than target.
If target is greater than or equal to the last character, the answer wraps around to letters[0].
Initialize l = 0, r = letters.length - 1. While l <= r: mid = (l + r) / 2. If letters[mid] <= target, l = mid + 1; else r = mid - 1. Return letters[l % letters.length].

brute.idea: Iterate linearly through letters from left to right to find the first character strictly greater than target.
steps: Iterate through each character c in letters.
If c > target, return c immediately.
If no character is strictly greater, return letters[0] (wrap-around).
brute.whySlow: Linear search inspects up to n characters instead of bisecting the sorted array.

optimal.idea: Upper-bound binary search finding the insertion index, wrapping around with modulo in O(log n) time.
steps: Initialize l = 0 and r = letters.length - 1.
While l <= r: let mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
If letters[mid] <= target, set l = mid + 1; else set r = mid - 1.
Return letters[l % letters.length].

whyNext: Builds on binary search boundary seeking from Search Insert Position (Seq 54) by searching the monotonic staircase formula k * (k + 1) / 2 <= n for the largest complete row count.
hints: A staircase of k complete rows requires k * (k + 1) / 2 coins.
Binary search for the maximum integer k in [0, n] such that k * (k + 1) / 2 <= n.
Set l = 0, r = n. While l <= r: mid = l + (r - l) / 2. Compute coins = mid * (mid + 1) / 2. If coins <= n: ans = mid, l = mid + 1; else r = mid - 1. Return ans.

brute.idea: Simulate row by row, subtracting row number i from n until remaining coins are insufficient.
steps: Initialize row = 1.
While n >= row: subtract row from n, then increment row.
Return row - 1 as the number of complete rows.
brute.whySlow: Simulating row by row takes O(sqrt(n)) time.

optimal.idea: Binary search on complete row count k in range [0, n] checking k * (k + 1) / 2 <= n in O(log n) time.
steps: Initialize l = 0 and r = n.
While l <= r: calculate mid = l + (r - l) / 2 and total = (long) mid * (mid + 1) / 2.
If total == n, return (int) mid.
If total < n, set l = (int) mid + 1; else set r = (int) mid - 1.
Return (int) r.

whyNext: Builds on binary search over sorted indices from Find Smallest Letter (Seq 343) by computing the count of missing numbers before index mid (arr[mid] - (mid + 1)) to locate the kth missing positive.
hints: At any index mid, the number of positive integers missing before arr[mid] is arr[mid] - (mid + 1).
Binary search for the index where missing count changes relative to k.
Initialize l = 0, r = arr.length - 1. While l <= r: mid = (l + r) / 2. If arr[mid] - (mid + 1) < k: l = mid + 1; else: r = mid - 1. The answer is l + k.

brute.idea: Iterate positive integers starting from 1; check if each is in arr, decrementing k on missing until k hits 0.
steps: Initialize cur = 1, idx = 0.
While k > 0: if idx < arr.length and arr[idx] == cur, idx++; else decrement k.
If k == 0, return cur.
Increment cur and repeat.
brute.whySlow: Iterating every positive integer takes O(n + k) time.

optimal.idea: Binary search on array indices using the invariant missingCount(mid) = arr[mid] - (mid + 1) in O(log n) time.
steps: Initialize l = 0 and r = arr.length - 1.
While l <= r: let mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
If arr[mid] - (mid + 1) < k, set l = mid + 1; else set r = mid - 1.
Return l + k.

whyNext: Builds on gradient bisection from Find Peak Element (Seq 59) by leveraging the strict bitonic structure of mountain arrays to locate the peak index in O(log n) time.
hints: Compare arr[mid] with arr[mid + 1] to determine which slope of the mountain you are on.
If arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1], you are on the ascending slope and the peak lies to the right.
Initialize l = 0, r = arr.length - 1. While l < r: mid = (l + r) / 2. If arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1], l = mid + 1; else r = mid. Return l.

brute.idea: Linearly scan the array to find the index of the maximum element.
steps: Iterate i from 1 to arr.length - 2.
If arr[i] > arr[i - 1] and arr[i] > arr[i + 1], return i.
Return peak index.
brute.whySlow: Linear scan inspects up to n elements in O(n) time.

optimal.idea: Binary search comparing arr[mid] and arr[mid + 1] to climb the mountain gradient in O(log n) time.
steps: Initialize l = 0 and r = arr.length - 1.
While l < r: calculate mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
If arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1], peak is to the right: set l = mid + 1.
Else: peak is at or to the left of mid: set r = mid.
Return l.

whyNext: Builds on binary search boundary navigation from Peak Index in a Mountain Array (Seq 346) by bisecting the starting index of a k-length window comparing distance to x from window endpoints.
hints: Instead of searching for elements directly, binary search for the left boundary of the k-element window.
The window can start anywhere from index 0 to n - k.
Set l = 0, r = arr.length - k. While l < r: mid = (l + r) / 2. If x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x, set l = mid + 1; else set r = mid. Return arr[l .. l + k - 1].

brute.idea: Sort elements by absolute difference from x, take the first k elements, and sort them back into natural order.
steps: Box array elements into a list.
Sort list using comparator: compare abs(a - x) and abs(b - x); tie-break with a - b.
Take first k elements from the sorted list.
Sort the k elements ascending and return.
brute.whySlow: Sorting the whole array takes O(n log n) time.

optimal.idea: Binary search on the window start index in range [0, n - k] comparing x - arr[mid] with arr[mid + k] - x in O(log(n - k) + k) time.
steps: Initialize l = 0 and r = arr.length - k.
While l < r: let mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
If x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x, window must shift right: l = mid + 1.
Else: window can remain at or left of mid: r = mid.
Collect elements arr[l .. l + k - 1] into a list and return.

whyNext: Builds on binary search on the answer from Koko Eating Bananas (Seq 63) by bisecting the divisor candidate range [1, max(nums)] to find the minimum divisor satisfying sum(ceil(num / d)) <= threshold.
hints: The answer is monotonic: larger divisors produce smaller sum totals.
Binary search the divisor d in range [1, max(nums)].
For a candidate mid, compute sum of (x + mid - 1) / mid. If sum <= threshold, try smaller divisor (r = mid - 1); else try larger (l = mid + 1).

brute.idea: Try every possible divisor starting from d = 1 upwards until sum(ceil(x / d)) <= threshold.
steps: Initialize d = 1.
Loop indefinitely: compute total = sum(ceil(x / d)) across all x in nums.
If total <= threshold, return d.
Increment d.
brute.whySlow: Iterating divisors linearly up to max(nums) takes O(max(nums) * n) time.

optimal.idea: Binary search the divisor range [1, max(nums)] with integer ceiling division in O(n log(max)) time.
steps: Find maxVal in nums.
Initialize l = 1, r = maxVal, ans = maxVal.
While l <= r: let mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
Compute sum of (x + mid - 1) / mid for all x in nums.
If sum <= threshold: ans = mid, r = mid - 1; else l = mid + 1.
Return ans.

whyNext: Builds on binary search on the answer from Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold (Seq 348) by bisecting the maximum allowed bag size M to verify if required split operations (ceil(balls / M) - 1) remain <= maxOperations.
hints: Binary search on the penalty (maximum balls in any bag) in range [1, max(nums)].
For a target bag size mid, the operations required to divide a bag with x balls is (x - 1) / mid.
Set l = 1, r = max(nums). While l <= r: mid = (l + r) / 2. If sum((x - 1) / mid) <= maxOperations: ans = mid, r = mid - 1; else l = mid + 1. Return ans.

brute.idea: Linear search testing each penalty size starting from 1 upwards until operations <= maxOperations.
steps: Initialize penalty = 1.
Compute operations needed: sum((x - 1) / penalty) for each x in nums.
If operations <= maxOperations, return penalty.
Increment penalty and repeat.
brute.whySlow: Testing all penalties linearly up to 10^9 takes O(max(nums) * n) time.

optimal.idea: Binary search on the penalty range [1, max(nums)] with operations formula (x - 1) / mid in O(n log(max)) time.
steps: Find maxVal in nums.
Initialize l = 1, r = maxVal, ans = maxVal.
While l <= r: mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
Compute totalOps = sum((x - 1) / mid) for all x in nums.
If totalOps <= maxOperations: ans = mid, r = mid - 1; else l = mid + 1.
Return ans.

whyNext: Combines array sorting with binary search thresholding from Find Smallest Letter (Seq 343) by sorting potions and using lower-bound binary search to count valid potion pairings for each spell.
hints: Sorting potions enables binary search to find the minimum potion strength needed for each spell.
For a spell with strength s, the minimum potion required is ceil(success / s).
Sort potions. For each spell: target = (success + spell - 1) / spell. Binary search for first potion >= target. Valid count is potions.length - idx.

brute.idea: For each spell, iterate through all potions and count how many produce a product >= success.
steps: Allocate result array pairs of size spells.length.
For each spell at index i, loop j through potions.
If (long) spells[i] * potions[j] >= success, increment count.
Assign pairs[i] = count.
Return pairs.
brute.whySlow: Scanning all potions for every spell takes O(n * m) time.

optimal.idea: Sort potions, then for each spell use binary search to locate the first potion >= ceil(success / spell) in O((m + n) log m) time.
steps: Sort potions in ascending order.
Initialize result array res of size spells.length.
For each spell: compute minPotion = (success + spell - 1) / spell.
Binary search in potions for the first index idx where potions[idx] >= minPotion.
Set res[i] = potions.length - idx.
Return res.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def successfulPairs(self, spells: list[int], potions: list[int], success: int) -> list[int]:
        import bisect
        potions.sort()
        m = len(potions)
        res = []
        for s in spells:
            min_potion = (success + s - 1) // s
            idx = bisect.bisect_left(potions, min_potion)
            res.append(m - idx)
        return res

whyNext: Builds on binary search on the answer from Minimum Limit of Balls in a Bag (Seq 349) by searching monotonic elapsed time T in [1, min(time) * totalTrips] to verify if sum(floor(T / t)) >= totalTrips.
hints: The more time allocated, the more trips the buses can complete in total; this relationship is strictly monotonic.
Binary search for the minimum elapsed time T in the search range [1, (long) min(time) * totalTrips].
Set l = 1, r = (long) minTime * totalTrips. While l <= r: mid = (l + r) / 2. Compute completed trips = sum(mid / t). If completed >= totalTrips, ans = mid, r = mid - 1; else l = mid + 1. Return ans.

brute.idea: Simulate time unit by unit, counting how many trips each bus has completed until the total reaches totalTrips.
steps: Initialize time = 1.
Loop indefinitely: compute trips = sum(time / t) across all bus durations.
If trips >= totalTrips, return time.
Increment time.
brute.whySlow: Simulating minute by minute takes O(answer * n) time, where answer can be up to 10^14.

optimal.idea: Binary search the time range [1, (long) min(time) * totalTrips] checking total trips in O(n log(min * totalTrips)) time.
steps: Find minTime among all buses.
Initialize l = 1 and r = (long) minTime * totalTrips, ans = r.
While l <= r: let mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
Calculate total completed = sum(mid / bus) for all buses in time.
If total >= totalTrips: ans = mid, r = mid - 1; else l = mid + 1.
Return ans.

whyNext: Builds on binary search on the answer from Minimum Time to Complete Trips (Seq 351) by bisecting pile size C in [1, max(candies)] to verify if sum(pile / C) >= k children.
hints: If each child can receive C candies, then each pile i can provide candies[i] // C children.
Binary search for the maximum candy pile size C in range [1, max(candies)].
Set l = 1, r = max(candies), ans = 0. While l <= r: mid = (l + r) / 2. Compute children = sum(c / mid). If children >= k: ans = mid, l = mid + 1; else r = mid - 1. Return ans.

brute.idea: Test each possible candy allocation per child starting from max(candies) downward until children served >= k.
steps: Find maxCandies in candies.
Iterate c from maxCandies down to 1.
Compute childrenServed = sum(pile / c).
If childrenServed >= k, return c.
Return 0 if no valid pile size found.
brute.whySlow: Linear search over pile sizes takes O(max(candies) * n) time.

optimal.idea: Binary search on candy allocation per child in range [1, max(candies)] in O(n log(max)) time.
steps: Find maxVal in candies.
Initialize l = 1, r = maxVal, ans = 0.
While l <= r: let mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
Calculate total children = sum(p / mid) for all piles.
If total >= k: ans = mid, l = mid + 1; else r = mid - 1.
Return ans.

whyNext: Builds on binary search thresholding from Successful Pairs of Spells and Potions (Seq 350) by storing values with strictly increasing timestamps in a HashMap of lists and using binary search to retrieve the latest timestamp <= target.
hints: Timestamps for any given key are strictly increasing, meaning the list of entries for each key is already sorted by timestamp.
Use binary search on the list of (timestamp, value) pairs for key to find the largest timestamp <= query timestamp.
In get(key, timestamp): retrieve list for key; if null return "". Binary search for the rightmost pair with pair.timestamp <= timestamp. If found return pair.value, else return "".

brute.idea: Store pairs in a HashMap of lists and linearly scan backwards to find the first timestamp <= target.
steps: Store entries as (timestamp, value) in a list under map[key].
In get(key, timestamp): iterate backwards through list.
Return value of first element with entry.timestamp <= timestamp.
If none found or key absent, return "".
brute.whySlow: Scanning backwards linearly takes O(m) time where m is number of entries under that key.

optimal.idea: Binary search over sorted timestamp entries for each key in O(log m) time per get query.
steps: Store (timestamp, value) in ArrayList under map[key]. Since timestamps arrive in strictly ascending order, list is pre-sorted.
In get(key, timestamp): binary search for the largest index with entry.timestamp <= timestamp.
Initialize l = 0, r = list.size() - 1, res = "".
While l <= r: mid = (l + r) / 2. If list[mid].timestamp <= timestamp: res = list[mid].value, l = mid + 1; else r = mid - 1.
Return res.
optimal.time: O(log m) per get, O(1) set

whyNext: Builds on binary search over sorted arrays from Median of Two Sorted Arrays (Seq 66) by binary searching the distance value D in [0, max - min] and counting pair distances <= D using a two-pointer sliding window.
hints: Sort the array: for any target distance D, you can count pairs with distance <= D in O(n) time using two pointers.
Binary search for the distance D in range [0, nums[n - 1] - nums[0]].
Set l = 0, r = max - min. While l < r: mid = (l + r) / 2. Count pairs (i, j) with nums[j] - nums[i] <= mid using sliding window. If count >= k, r = mid; else l = mid + 1. Return l.

brute.idea: Generate all n * (n - 1) / 2 pair distances, sort them, and return the k-th smallest element.
steps: Calculate difference abs(nums[i] - nums[j]) for all pairs (i, j) with i < j.
Store all differences in an array of size n(n - 1)/2.
Sort the differences array.
Return the element at index k - 1.
brute.whySlow: Generating and sorting all O(n²) distances takes O(n² log n) time and O(n²) space.

optimal.idea: Binary search the distance range [0, max - min], using two pointers to count pairs with diff <= mid in O(n log(max - min)) time.
steps: Sort nums in ascending order.
Initialize l = 0 and r = nums[nums.length - 1] - nums[0].
While l < r: let mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
Count pairs with distance <= mid: initialize count = 0, left = 0; for right from 0 to n - 1: while nums[right] - nums[left] > mid, increment left; count += right - left.
If count >= k: r = mid; else l = mid + 1.
Return l.
optimal.time: O(n log n + n log(max - min))
